lesson.title: The Event Horizon
lesson.objective: Understand why nothing, not even light, escapes from inside the event horizon.
lesson.approachReason: The learner predicts and experiments with escape speed before the terms 'speed of light limit' and 'event horizon' are ever named, so the key insight is earned rather than told.

blocks.heading: The speed you need to leave forever
blocks.body:
Throw a ball up and gravity pulls it back. Throw it faster and it climbs higher before turning around. Past a certain speed — the escape speed — it never turns around at all: it coasts away and simply never returns.

For any object that speed is set by only two things: how much mass is pulling, and how close to the center you start. Escape speed grows as 1/√r. Halve the radius and you need 1.41× the speed; quarter the radius and you need 2×. Make the radius tiny and the required speed climbs without limit.
blocks.example: Earth's escape speed is 11.2 km/s (about 40,000 km/h). A rocket doesn't have to hit that in one instant — it can keep burning — but a thrown ball, or a beam of light, only gets one shot.

hints: Escape speed depends on mass and on how close you start to the center — not on how far you have to travel.
If two objects have the same mass, the smaller one has the higher escape speed, and the gap grows as 1/√r.
blocks.retry: Picture the gravity well as a valley. Same mass means the same depth, but a smaller radius puts your feet on a steeper wall — a short climb, but a brutal one.

blocks.heading: The one speed nothing can beat
blocks.body:
Escape speed grows without limit as you squeeze — but the universe has a ceiling. Nothing can travel faster than the speed of light: c = 300,000 km/s.

So something remarkable happens if you compress an object enough. There is a radius where the escape speed equals c. At that radius — and everywhere inside it — no rocket, no particle, and no beam of light can ever climb out. That boundary is the event horizon.

An event horizon is not a surface or a wall. It is a region of space where every route outward is closed. Light inside it can still move — it just can't move outward.
blocks.example: The horizon is small for stellar masses: roughly 3 km for every solar mass. A 10-solar-mass black hole has a horizon about 30 km in radius — the size of a small city, yet completely sealed.

hints: Ask what the escape speed is at that radius, and compare it with the fastest speed anything can have.
The horizon is a boundary in space, not an object with a surface — matter passing it notices nothing solid.
blocks.retry: Think of a one-way door built into space itself. Outside it you can still leave if you are fast enough; at the door, the exit speed required is the fastest speed the universe allows; inside, every road bends back toward the center.

blocks.heading: How fast is escape from a crushed Earth?
blocks.prompt: Earth's escape speed at its present radius is 11.2 km/s. Suppose the whole Earth — same mass — were somehow squeezed down to one hundredth of its current radius. What would the escape speed from its new surface be, in km/s?

traps.feedback: You scaled linearly with the radius change. Escape speed goes as 1/√r, so a 100× shrink is only a 10× increase.
That divides by 100. Squeezing the same mass smaller makes escape harder, not easier.
That is the answer for a 4× shrink. Here the radius drops by a factor of 100, so √100 = 10.

hints: Escape speed scales with 1/√r: a factor-of-4 shrink only doubles it.
The radius shrinks by 100, and √100 = 10, so multiply 11.2 km/s by 10.
blocks.solution: Escape speed is √(2GM/r), so it changes as 1/√r. Shrinking the radius by 100 multiplies the speed by √100 = 10: 11.2 × 10 = 112 km/s. Even that is less than 0.04% of the speed of light — you would have to shrink the Earth by hundreds of millions of times more before your planet became a black hole.

hints: Compare 250,000 km/s with the speed of light, 300,000 km/s.
Escape speed rises with mass. What happens when it finally passes c?
blocks.retry: Escape speed is a tug-of-war: mass pulls harder, distance from the center weakens the pull. Add mass, or shrink the radius, and you tip the balance toward trapping light.

blocks.heading: Why is a black hole black?
blocks.prompt: Explain to a friend, in your own words, why a black hole looks black. Use the idea of escape speed — and don't just say "because its gravity is strong."
blocks.model: A strong model answer: escape speed depends on mass and on how close you start to the center. Pack enough mass into a small enough radius and, at some distance, the speed needed to get away reaches the speed of light. Inside that distance, even a beam aimed straight outward makes no headway — it is like swimming against a current faster than you can swim. No light ever reaches our telescopes from inside, so we see nothing there: a black hole.

activities.title: Escape speeds, from the Moon to a neutron star
activities.prompt: Here are six real objects, sorted by nothing at all. Before you see the numbers, guess which one has the highest escape speed — then check the bars.
activities.reveal: Even the Sun, with 333,000 Earth-masses, only needs 617.5 km/s to escape — about 0.2% of light speed. It takes a fantastically compressed object, like a neutron star, to push escape speed anywhere near c. Compress a little further and you cross the line.

bars.label: Moon
bars.note: A small, light world — a modest 2.4 km/s gets you away.

bars.label: Mars
bars.note: Roughly twice the Moon's escape speed at 5.0 km/s.

bars.label: Earth
bars.note: 11.2 km/s — the fastest any crewed rocket has ever needed to reach.

bars.label: Jupiter
bars.note: 318 Earth-masses, but a huge radius too: escape speed is 59.5 km/s.

bars.label: Sun
bars.note: 617.5 km/s — still only about 0.2% of the speed of light.

bars.label: Neutron star (1.4 solar masses, 10 km radius)
bars.note: About 190,000 km/s — over 60% of light speed, from an object the size of a city.

activities.title: Squeeze a 10-solar-mass core
activities.prompt: Drag the slider to set the radius of a collapsed core holding 10 times the Sun's mass. Watch how the escape speed changes as you crush it smaller.
activities.reveal: There is a critical radius — 30 km here — where the escape speed exactly equals the speed of light. At that radius and anything inside it, nothing gets out. That radius is the event horizon.

bands.title: Inside the horizon
bands.detail: At 30 km the escape speed is exactly 300,000 km/s — the speed of light. Crush it further and the escape speed exceeds c: not even a beam of light can climb out.

bands.title: Relativistic escape
bands.detail: Between 30 and 60 km, escape needs 0.7 to 1.0 times the speed of light. No rocket could ever do it, but light still gets out.

bands.title: Fast, but well below light speed
bands.detail: At 100 km the escape speed is about 163,000 km/s — roughly half of light speed. Extreme, but this core is not yet a black hole.

questions.question: A cargo hauler must launch a pod off the surface of one of two moons so that it never falls back. Both moons have exactly the same mass: Moon Barek has a radius of 500 km and Moon Tolan has a radius of 2,000 km. Which launch needs the higher escape speed?
options: Moon Barek — same mass but a smaller radius means a higher escape speed
Moon Tolan — the pod has farther to climb, so it needs more speed
They are identical, because escape speed depends only on the moon's mass
Neither is fixed — the escape speed depends on the pod's own mass
questions.correctAnswer: Moon Barek — same mass but a smaller radius means a higher escape speed
questions.explanation: Escape speed is √(2GM/r): it depends on the mass pulling and on how close you start to the center, not on how far you travel. With equal masses, shrinking the radius by 4 raises the required speed by √4 = 2, so tiny Barek is the harder launch.

questions.question: A 10-solar-mass star collapses until its surface sits 30 km from the center. At that radius the escape speed is 300,000 km/s — the speed of light. Which statement is correct?
options: Light can still leave the surface, but it will be strongly redshifted
Nothing that starts at or inside 30 km can get out — no rocket, no particle, no light
A powerful enough rocket can still escape, because rockets carry their own fuel
The 30 km boundary is a solid surface that light bounces off
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing that starts at or inside 30 km can get out — no rocket, no particle, no light
questions.explanation: At 30 km the escape speed equals the fastest speed the universe allows, so anything starting there or deeper cannot reach the outside. The boundary is the event horizon — a region of space, not a solid shell.

questions.question: A collapsed star has a surface escape speed of 250,000 km/s. Astronomers then add mass to it while its radius stays the same. What is true now?
options: It is already a black hole — nothing can escape from its surface
Light can still escape right now, but a little more mass or a little more squeezing would push the escape speed past the speed of light
Escape speed can never exceed the speed of light, so it can never become a black hole
Adding mass has no effect on escape speed; only the radius matters
questions.correctAnswer: Light can still escape right now, but a little more mass or a little more squeezing would push the escape speed past the speed of light
questions.explanation: Escape speed is √(2GM/r), so it rises with mass and rises as the radius shrinks. At 250,000 km/s light still gets out — barely — and pushing past 300,000 km/s is exactly what creates an event horizon.
